item.title: 3: Daily Halacha: Hames in One's House on Pesah
item.description:
What does the Torah require us to do with Hames before Pesah? Beyond the ban on eating, there are prohibitions of seeing and finding Hames in one's possession, and a positive misvah to dispose of it from midday on Erev Pesah. The ban covers only Hames one owns; sealed Hames in the house is permitted.

item.description:

item.title: 10: Daily Halacha: Disposing of Hames
item.description:
What is the punishment for eating hames on Pesah, and when is it disposed of when Erev Pesah is Shabbat? Karet applies to the seven days, while from midday on Erev Pesah it is forbidden without karet. Hames may be eaten until 10 on Shabbat morning, the rest disposed of by 11 on Friday.

item.description:
Which foods need a hekhsher on Pesah? Part 2 explains that for Sephardim, following the Shulhan Arukh, the main stringency is that Hames does not become nullified, so natural items like salt, sugar, tea, coffee and oil need no hekhsher if bought before Pesah. The Rema is stricter for Ashkenazim, who seemingly would require one.

item.title: 76: Daily Halacha: Drinking and Eating During the Seder and When to Eat the Egg
item.description:
May you eat and drink during the Seder, and when should the egg be eaten? After Kiddush you may drink tea, coffee or water without a berakhah, but not anything intoxicating. Eating should be limited to under a kezayit unless needed to concentrate, and the egg is best eaten during the meal.

item.title: 77: Daily Halacha: Pouring Wine During the 10 Plagues and Avoiding Superstitions
item.description:
Why do we pour out wine at each of the ten plagues? The custom goes back to the Rokeah in thirteenth-century Germany and spread to Sephardim through the Arizal. It carries sadness over the Egyptians and a wish that the plagues not fall on us, but the shiur warns against the superstitions that grew around it.

item.title: 78: Daily Halacha: Women in Haggadah and Does Everyone Need to Read the Haggadah?
item.description:
Are women obligated to read the Haggadah, and does everyone have to read every word? Women are equally obligated in telling the story, since the poskim see it as a Torah duty. It is fulfilled by one person reading and explaining while others listen and understand, with key passages translated and the Haggadah used as a springboard for discussion.
